title: Social complexity and multiagency care
blurb: Give women with complex social factors the extra, coordinated care NICE CG110 sets out, while you keep providing their midwifery care.
question: A woman who is an asylum seeker attends for her first antenatal contact at 22 weeks. She speaks little English and her husband offers to interpret. What should the midwife do first?

teach.h: What counts as a complex social factor
teach.body: NICE CG110 gives examples of complex social factors in pregnancy: poverty, homelessness, substance misuse, recent arrival as a migrant, asylum seeker or refugee status, difficulty speaking or understanding English, age under 20 and domestic abuse. These women are less likely to use antenatal care and are at higher risk of poor outcomes. In plain English: the same pregnancy can carry very different risks depending on a woman's life, so the midwife adapts the service to reach her.

teach.h: CG110: the key action for each group
head: Group
What the midwife offers
rows: Referral at first disclosure; named specialist midwife or doctor
Named midwife giving most of her care
Confidential record; info card; flexible appointments
At least one consultation without partner or family
teach.caption: Every woman also gets an out-of-hours number at booking (CG110 1.1.13).

teach.h: Collaborate, but keep being her midwife
teach.body: SPM 4.9 asks midwives to work with interdisciplinary and multiagency teams while continuing to provide the midwifery care women and babies need. Consider a multiagency needs assessment, including safeguarding, so she has one coordinated care plan. Respect her confidentiality, discuss her fears without judgement, and tell her why and when information about her pregnancy may need to be shared with other agencies. A referral adds support; it does not hand her care to someone else.

teach.caption: Text reminders for appointments and help with transport support attendance (CG110 1.2.8, 1.2.11).

Safeguarding for her and the baby

teach.h: Creating a safe space to disclose
teach.caption: NICE NG201 1.2.5; CG110 1.1.14, 1.5.8, 1.5.10 (credit card-sized helpline card).

teach.body: Hana, an asylum seeker, comes to the community clinic at 22 weeks with no booking. Her husband offers to interpret. Midwife Ruth books a professional interpreter instead, allows extra time, and explains antenatal care and Hana's entitlement to it. She records a current address and phone number, asks Hana to report any move, and checks understanding by asking Hana to explain the plan back. She arranges booking bloods and screening and plans a one-to-one appointment.

rows.label: Homelessness: register with a GP without proof of address
Learning disability: reasonable adjustments and accessible information
Moving area: she takes a copy of her hand-held notes
Concern for the unborn baby: share information lawfully, keep caring

teach.note: Equality Act 2010 s20; Accessible Information Standard; CG110 1.1.5.

teach.text: A partner, family member or legal guardian should not interpret for her: use a professional interpreter, link worker or advocate. And a safeguarding or social care referral does not end your role: she still needs her midwife.

items: CG110 complex social factors include poverty, homelessness, substance misuse, migrant or asylum status, little English, age under 20 and domestic abuse.
Offer substance misuse referral at first disclosure and a named specialist midwife or doctor with a direct line.
Professional interpreter, never a partner or relative; longer appointments; check understanding.
Under 20s and women experiencing domestic abuse get a named midwife providing most of their care.
See every woman alone at least once; domestic abuse goes in a confidential record, not the hand-held notes.

summary: You can now recognise complex social factors and offer the specific extra care NICE CG110 recommends for each group. You can also work with other agencies and share information appropriately while continuing to give the woman her midwifery care.

A.q: A woman who speaks very little English attends for booking with her sister, who speaks fluent English and offers to translate. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Accept her sister's offer to translate
Use a professional interpreter
Give her written leaflets in English
Rebook once her English improves
A.why: CG110 1.3.10: provide an interpreter (who may be a link worker or advocate) who is not a family member, legal guardian or partner, in her preferred language.

whyNot.0: Family members should not interpret: she may not disclose sensitive issues and accuracy cannot be assured.
whyNot.2: English leaflets do not meet her language need and do not check understanding.
whyNot.3: Delaying booking puts her and the baby at risk; care must be accessible now.

A.q: At her first antenatal contact, a woman tells the midwife she uses heroin daily. What should the midwife offer first?
options: A referral to children's social care
An urgent appointment with her GP
Referral to a substance misuse programme
Advice to stop heroin use immediately
A.why: CG110 1.2.7: the first time a woman who misuses substances discloses she is pregnant, offer referral to an appropriate substance misuse programme.

whyNot.0: Safeguarding may be needed, but the recommended first offer is the substance misuse programme within coordinated care.
whyNot.1: A GP appointment does not provide the specialist substance misuse support CG110 recommends.
whyNot.3: Abrupt advice without specialist support is not the recommended response and may be unsafe.

A.q: A 17-year-old attends for booking at 10 weeks. According to NICE CG110, what should she be offered?
options: Shared care led by her GP
A referral to a consultant obstetrician
Care in the hospital antenatal clinic
A named midwife who provides most of her care
A.why: CG110 1.4.4: offer young women under 20 a named midwife who takes responsibility for and provides the majority of her antenatal care, with a direct-line number.

whyNot.0: GP-led shared care is not the CG110 recommendation for women under 20.
whyNot.1: Age alone is not an indication for consultant-led care.
whyNot.2: CG110 favours age-appropriate care in the community rather than hospital clinics.

B.q: A woman discloses domestic abuse at a community antenatal appointment. Where should the midwife record the disclosure?
options: In a confidential record kept separately
In her hand-held maternity notes
In a letter given to the woman
On the summary page of her notes
B.why: CG110 1.5.8: tell the woman the information she discloses will be kept in a confidential record and not included in her hand-held record.

whyNot.1: The perpetrator may read hand-held notes, putting her at greater risk.
whyNot.2: A letter she carries home could be found by the perpetrator.
whyNot.3: The summary page travels with the hand-held notes and is not confidential.

B.q: A woman at 20 weeks has attended every appointment with her partner, who answers most questions for her. What should the midwife arrange?
options: A home visit with both partners present
A referral to the police
A consultation with the woman on her own
A telephone call to the partner
B.why: CG110 1.1.14: provide each woman with a one-to-one consultation without her partner, a family member or a legal guardian present on at least one occasion, to allow discussion of sensitive issues.

whyNot.0: A joint home visit still gives her no private space to disclose.
whyNot.1: There is no disclosure or evidence yet that would justify a police referral.
whyNot.3: Speaking to the partner does not give the woman a safe space to talk.

B.q: A pregnant woman who uses cannabis and alcohol says she is frightened that social services will take her baby. Which response best follows NICE CG110?
options: Tell her social services will not be involved
Give her tailored information about what to expect
Suggest she avoids mentioning her drug use
Advise her to discuss it with a solicitor
B.why: CG110 1.2.1 and 1.2.10: address women's fears about children's services by giving information tailored to their needs, including what care the baby may need and any potential involvement of social services.

whyNot.0: This may be untrue; the midwife cannot promise that social services will not be involved.
whyNot.2: Concealment is unsafe and against the Code's duty of honesty.
whyNot.3: Legal advice is not the midwife's role here; tailored information and support are.

C.q: A refugee at 30 weeks tells the midwife she is being moved to accommodation in another city next week. Which action best maintains her care?
options: Discharge her from the current maternity service
Ask her new GP to request her records later
Book her into the new unit once she arrives
Give her a copy of her hand-held notes to take
C.why: CG110 1.1.5 and 1.3.8: women should be able to take a copy of their hand-held notes when moving area, and keep them with them at all times; the midwife also confirms contact details (1.1.12).

whyNot.0: Discharging her without a handover risks a gap in care at 30 weeks.
whyNot.1: Waiting for a records request leaves her new team without information.
whyNot.2: Booking on arrival is helpful but without her notes the new team lacks her history and results.

C.q: A woman with a learning disability attends for an antenatal appointment with her support worker. Which approach best meets her needs?
options: Direct questions to her support worker
Give her the standard written leaflet
Offer a longer appointment and easy read information
Refer her to a consultant for all decisions
C.why: The Equality Act 2010 s20 requires reasonable adjustments, and the Accessible Information Standard requires information in a format she can use. Speak to her directly and allow more time.

whyNot.0: Talking over her to the support worker fails to respect her as the decision maker.
whyNot.1: A standard leaflet may not be accessible to her.
whyNot.3: A learning disability does not remove her right to make her own decisions.

C.q: A midwife makes a safeguarding referral for an unborn baby. The woman is upset and asks whether she will still see her midwife. What is the best response?
options: Her midwifery care continues alongside the referral
Her care will now be led by the social worker
Her appointments will pause until the assessment
Her care will move to a different midwifery team
C.why: SPM 4.9: the midwife works with multiagency teams while continuing to provide the midwifery care the woman and baby need; CG110 1.1.9 says to explain why and when information is shared.

whyNot.1: Social workers coordinate safeguarding, not her midwifery care.
whyNot.2: Pausing antenatal care would put mother and baby at risk.
whyNot.3: There is no reason to change team; continuity supports engagement.

reteach.title: Same pregnancy, different doors
reteach.question: Why do some women not come through the front door of maternity care, and how do you open other doors?

blocks.h: Remove the barrier, keep the care
blocks.body: Language, fear of social services, embarrassment, a controlling partner, a missing address: each is a barrier to care. CG110 removes them: an interpreter, tailored information, a named midwife, a private appointment, notes she carries. The midwife works with other agencies but stays her midwife throughout.

blocks.h: Barrier and the door you open
head: Barrier
Door

blocks.text: Family interpreters and partner-present appointments are the two classic ways disclosure is silenced.

explain.body: CG110 lists poverty, homelessness, substance misuse, recent migration, asylum or refugee status, difficulty with English, age under 20 and domestic abuse as complex social factors.

test.q: Which of these is listed by NICE CG110 as an example of a complex social factor in pregnancy?
options: Age under 25
First pregnancy
Age under 20
Previous caesarean
test.why: CG110 1.1.1 includes age under 20 among its examples of complex social factors.

whyNot.1: A first pregnancy is a clinical factor, not a complex social factor.
whyNot.3: A previous caesarean is an obstetric history factor.

explain.body: At first contact and booking, ask her to report any change of address and give her a number to use. At booking, give an out-of-hours number such as triage, the labour ward or the birth centre.

test.q: What does NICE CG110 recommend giving every woman at her booking appointment?
options: A food voucher application
A telephone number for out-of-hours contact
A referral to a health visitor
A copy of the trust's complaints policy
test.why: CG110 1.1.13: give the woman a telephone number to contact a healthcare professional outside normal working hours, such as triage, the labour ward or birth centre.

whyNot.0: Food vouchers are not a CG110 booking recommendation.
whyNot.2: Health visitor contact is arranged later in the pathway, not at booking for every woman.
whyNot.3: A complaints policy is not the CG110 recommendation.

explain.body: When an interpreter is used, services should offer flexibility in the number and length of appointments, over and above the routine schedule, and check her understanding of spoken information.

test.q: A woman needs an interpreter for her antenatal care. How should the appointment schedule be planned?
options: Fewer appointments to limit interpreter costs
Standard appointments as for other women
Telephone appointments in place of visits
Longer and more flexible appointments
test.why: CG110 1.3.4: offer flexibility in the number and length of antenatal appointments when interpreting services are used.

whyNot.1: Standard-length appointments do not allow time for interpretation.
whyNot.2: CG110 does not recommend replacing visits with phone calls.

explain.body: A person does not need ID, proof of address or immigration status to register with a GP; a temporary or surgery address can be used. Helping her register supports care after the birth too.

test.q: A pregnant woman who is sofa-surfing says she cannot register with a GP because she has no fixed address. What should the midwife tell her?
options: She can register using a temporary address
She must first obtain a council tenancy
She should use the emergency department instead
She needs photo ID before registering
test.why: NHS guidance: no ID, proof of address or immigration status is needed to register with a GP; a temporary or surgery address can be used.

whyNot.1: A tenancy is not required to register.
whyNot.2: The emergency department is not a substitute for primary care.
whyNot.3: Photo ID is not required to register with a GP.
